body:
Sign in to Slack from radar instead of pasting a token. Getting a user token today means making a Slack app from the manifest and copying its token, which is a lot to ask of anyone else; signing in gives them the same long-lived user token in a few clicks. Depends on #43 for the redirect.

**Flow:** setup's Slack step and Settings → Slack → connection offer **sign in**. radar opens Slack's authorise page (radar's app, PKCE, user scopes only, token rotation off, the relay page as redirect), catches the code on `127.0.0.1`, exchanges it with the verifier, and runs the usual check (who, scopes).

**Token:** the returned `xoxp-` user token is kept where a pasted token is kept today, and used the same way. **Sign out** calls `auth.revoke` and removes it.

**Pasted tokens:** `env:NAME` and pasted `xoxp-` keep working, for workspaces that block distributed apps and for people who make their own app.

**Manifest:** add `pkce_enabled` and the redirect URL; the copy-the-manifest path for self-made apps stays.

**Admin page** (from #45): a short page a user can send to the workspace admin who approves radar's app. It maps each requested user scope to the feature that uses it (from `NEEDS` in `crates/radar-slack/src/settings.rs`), marks `chat:write` and `reactions:write` optional (without them radar only reads), says radar reads as the signed-in user with no bot, and says what radar keeps locally.

**Done when:**
- sign in and sign out work against a recorded or faked Slack (no live calls in tests, `RADAR_SANDBOX` opens no browser);
- the token appears in no log or view data;
- `docs/user-guide/connect.md#slack` describes sign-in, and the admin page is linked from it.

milestone.title: Slack sign-in rework
milestone.description:
Replace the pasted long-lived Slack user token with a sign-in from radar: PKCE OAuth through an HTTPS relay page, rotating tokens kept out of the config file, and a sign-in that runs out after an interval radar sets.

**Status:** radar has one user today, who already has a working token. This milestone is the plan for when someone else wants to connect Slack; adapt it to what they need then. The channel list (first issue) is useful now.

## Today

Each person makes their own Slack app from radar's manifest (`crates/radar-slack/src/manifest.rs`, 10 user scopes, no bot scopes), installs it (in most company workspaces that is "Request to Install" and an admin approves it, once per person), copies the `xoxp-` token, and pastes it or exports it (`env:SLACK_TOKEN`). The token never expires; a pasted one is saved in plain text in the config file. Channels are added by pasting a link or id.

## What Slack's documentation says (checked 2026-10-21)

- **PKCE is generally available** (changelog 2026-03-30). `oauth.v2.access` takes `code` + `code_verifier` and no `client_secret`. Turned on in app settings or with `pkce_enabled: true` in the manifest's `oauth_config`. One-way: only Slack support can turn it off. With PKCE on, refresh tokens expire after 30 days.
- **Redirects:** a server redirect must be HTTPS. With PKCE on, `http://localhost:<port>/…` counts as a desktop redirect; desktop redirects cannot ask for bot scopes (radar asks for none).
- **Token rotation:** access tokens expire after 12 hours; refresh tokens are single use and each refresh returns a new one; works for user tokens; `auth.revoke` cancels one token; rotation cannot be turned off once on.
- **Shared app:** "Once an app is installed, all members of the workspace can connect their accounts to use it", and with approval on, "Members can install any apps approved by a Workspace Owner". Connecting a member means running OAuth, so this only helps together with the sign-in. An app without distribution cannot be installed in other workspaces (`invalid_team_for_non_distributed_app`); distribution asks for SSL on redirect URLs.
- **Scopes** are additive across sign-ins and cannot be removed without revoking. Admins can approve a subset of an app's scopes. Unclear whether adding a scope later needs a second approval, so a read-only-first manifest was dropped in favour of one manifest whose write scopes an admin may leave out.

## Design

- radar owns one distributed app with PKCE and rotation on; its client id is in the binary. A workspace admin approves it once; every member then signs in from radar.
- Redirect: a static HTTPS page (GitHub Pages) forwards `code` and `state` to radar's listener on `127.0.0.1:<port>` (the port travels in `state`), or shows the code to paste if the hop fails. The page holds nothing; a code is useless without the verifier only radar has.
- Access token in memory only. Refresh token in the OS keychain (macOS Keychain, Secret Service on Linux), never the config file; with no keychain, memory only (sign in at each start).
- radar's own sign-in interval, a setting (default 1 day; 7 and 30 days offered). When it passes radar drops the refresh token and the Slack status reads signed out with a key to sign in; held messages stay readable, other parts keep working.
- Sign out calls `auth.revoke` and clears the keychain entry.
- The manifest-and-paste path stays for workspaces that block distributed apps; setup marks a pasted token as long-lived.

## Order

1. Channel list from the channels you are in.
2. Spike: PKCE through the HTTPS relay with a throwaway app.
3. Sign-in step: rotation, keychain, interval, revoke.
4. A page for workspace admins.

## Sources

- https://docs.slack.dev/authentication/using-pkce
- https://docs.slack.dev/changelog/2026/03/30/pkce
- https://docs.slack.dev/authentication/using-token-rotation
- https://docs.slack.dev/authentication/installing-with-oauth
- https://docs.slack.dev/app-management/distribution/
- https://docs.slack.dev/admins/managing-app-approvals
- https://slack.com/help/articles/222386767-Manage-app-approval-for-your-workspace
- https://slack.com/help/articles/202035138-Add-apps-to-your-Slack-workspace

title: Slack: sign in from radar (PKCE, long-lived user token)

body:
Prove the sign-in redirect before building it, with a throwaway Slack app and a scratch crate (not in the workspace). The sign-in exists so people other than the maintainer can get a user token without making their own app; the token it returns is the same long-lived `xoxp-` a pasted one is.

**Set up:**
- a Slack app with only user scopes, PKCE on, token rotation off, public distribution on;
- a static relay page on GitHub Pages: reads `code` and `state`, takes the port from `state`, sends the browser to `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/slack?code=…&state=…`; if that fails, shows the code to paste;
- ~50 lines of Rust: listener on `127.0.0.1:0`, verifier and challenge, open the authorise URL with `user_scope=…` and the relay as `redirect_uri`, check `state`, call `oauth.v2.access` with `code` + `code_verifier` and no secret, then `auth.test` and `auth.revoke`.

**Questions to answer (each with what was seen):**
1. Does `oauth.v2.access` accept a verifier and no secret when the redirect is HTTPS (a server redirect), not localhost? Slack documents PKCE mostly for desktop redirects.
2. Does public distribution accept the HTTPS relay as the redirect URL? (If 1 fails: does it accept a `http://localhost` redirect?)
3. Does the hop from the HTTPS page to `http://127.0.0.1` work in Chrome, Firefox and Safari without a prompt or block (local network access rules)?
4. With rotation off, is the returned user token long-lived (no `expires_in`, no refresh token)?

**Done when:** the answers are written in this issue, and the sign-in issue is updated with the redirect that works. Delete the throwaway app afterwards. Record nothing with a real token in it.

body:
Every icon gets the same two cells whatever the pack (nerd, unicode, emoji, off), so changing pack never moves a column. Today the slot is the pack's own width, 0, 1 or 2 cells (`icon_width` in the look the host sends, `design::icon` pack width; text/look.ts iconWidth), so changing pack still moves columns (state on 2026-10-22, alpha.16). Emoji width is unreliable across terminals and tmux; decide whether the emoji pack measures width at start or goes.

Host-led: Look/icon width semantics and every column calculation (the host's `view::measure` and Ink's columns).

Done when switching between all four packs leaves every column where it was.

Design: Ink style guide, sheet 03.

Ink is the only renderer since alpha.14 (#26).
title: Fixed two-cell icon slot in every pack

body:
Colour code in diffs, markdown code blocks and the editor with shiki 4.5 (MIT, +614 KB). A spike confirmed the JS regex engine works without WASM and codeToTokens gives a colour and style per token, per line. First TypeScript highlight ~250 ms while its grammar compiles, then 2–60 ms. Bundle only the languages radar shows.

Theme: add syntax.* slots (keyword, string, number, comment, type, function) to the host's look so users can recolour code; build the shiki theme from them. On no colour, skip shiki and draw text.primary.

Where: ink/src/text/code.ts.

Done when a Rust and a TypeScript diff are coloured from the slots.

Design: Ink style guide, sheets 05 and 09.

Ink is the only renderer since alpha.14 (#26).
title: Code colours with shiki and syntax.* theme slots

body:
Show a GitLab pipeline as a graph: stages as columns, jobs as boxes bordered in their state, needs as lines, the chosen job on the selection shade, ⏎ opens its log. On a narrow screen fall back to the stage list with only failed or running jobs open.

Library: @dagrejs/dagre 3.1.1 (MIT, +71 KB). A spike laid out the pipeline in cell units and drew it cleanly with a connection-bitmask rasteriser in 35–50 ms warm; skip-stage edges need routing work.

Host: a graph node with jobs, state and needs. Ink: nodes/graph.tsx, which owns the layout.

Done when a real pipeline draws as a graph at 160×40 and falls back to the list at 80×24.

Design: Ink style guide, sheet 05 and 09.

Ink is the only renderer since alpha.14 (#26).
title: Pipeline graph view, laid out with @dagrejs/dagre
